source_read: PMC HTML full text, PMC2835832 (author manuscript of Drug Alcohol Depend 2010;108(1-2):84-97), read in full in the reader's own browser tab: Abstract, Introduction, Method, Results, Discussion, Limitations, Conclusions, and Tables 1-5 as HTML tables with their footnotes. The supplementary tables (a .doc file) were not opened (download link). No funding or conflict-of-interest statement appears in the PMC text.

claims.overstatement: None material. Precision: (1) 'surveys in 17 countries ... dependence in the 17-country surveys': the drug-dependence models could only use 11 of the 17 surveys, because age of onset of drug dependence was not assessed in Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and Spain; the tobacco-dependence model used 7. (2) The 0.2-0.7 range spans all five outcomes, including alcohol dependence (0.5) and tobacco dependence (0.7); for drug dependence among people who had used cannabis, cocaine or other illegal drugs it is 0.2 to 0.5. (3) 'Age at first use' is the age of first use of the drug concerned (Table 5 footnote), although the text speaks of earlier onset of exposure to drugs overall. The claim's 'went with' and its causal caveat fit a cross-sectional design with recalled ages.
claims.note: Checked against Table 5: age of onset of use, odds ratios (95% CI) alcohol dependence 0.5 (0.4-0.7), tobacco dependence 0.7 (0.6-0.8), drug dependence among people who used cannabis 0.2 (0.2-0.3), cocaine 0.5 (0.3-0.7), other illegal drugs 0.3 (0.2-0.4); range 0.2-0.7 confirmed; the unit (per year or otherwise) is not stated anywhere. These are adjusted estimates from multivariable discrete-time survival models: sex, age at interview, number of internalising and of externalising disorders by age 15, years since first use, tobacco and alcohol use, number of illegal drug classes used (time-varying), the three order violations, and country. More drug classes went with higher odds (for example drug dependence among people who used cannabis: 6.1, 15.4 and 35.7 for 2, 3 and 4 classes vs 1). Order violations: no significant association except other illegal drugs before cannabis for alcohol dependence (1.6, 1.1-2.3), which fits 'largely'. Dependence means onset of the full DSM-IV dependence syndrome (CIDI 3.0), with ages of onset recalled at the single interview.

anchors.locator: Table 5, rows 'Number of illicit drugs used' and 'Gateway violation' with footnote 4
anchors.extracted: Number of illegal drug classes used (time-varying; cannabis, cocaine, prescription drugs, other) vs one class, drug dependence among people who used cannabis: 2 classes 6.1 (4.5-8.3), 3 classes 15.4 (11.1-21.5), 4 classes 35.7 (24.6-51.8); similar gradients for the other outcomes. The three order violations were not significantly associated with any dependence outcome, except other illegal drugs before cannabis for alcohol dependence, 1.6 (1.1-2.3).

anchors.locator: Method › 2.2 Measures, 2nd paragraph; Table 5 footnotes 5 and 6
anchors.extracted: Age of onset of drug dependence not assessed in Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and Spain, so the drug-dependence models draw on 11 of the 17 surveys; nicotine dependence not assessed in 10 countries, leaving 7 for the tobacco-dependence model.

17 countries (7 developing, 10 developed), household probability samples, national in most but regional in China, Colombia, Japan and Mexico; 85,088 respondents; weighted average response 69.9% (45.9% France to 87.7% Colombia); fieldwork 2001-2005 (Table 1); face-to-face lay interviews; substance use assessed in the Part II subsample, weighted back to the population.

Cross-sectional surveys not designed for this question; ages of first use recalled retrospectively, decades later for older respondents; repeat assessments in other studies show recalled ages rise with time, though the reported order does not change.

The authors suggest that the risk of later dependence may depend more on how much any drug has been used before and on the age at which use began than on which drug came first, and note that early-onset internalising and externalising disorders also predicted dependence.

claims.overstatement: Not supported as worded: (1) 'cannabis use usually came before other illegal drugs, except where cannabis was rare': the order also broke down where cannabis use was moderate. In South Africa, where 8.5% had used cannabis by 29 (the paper calls this moderate; cross-country median 9.8%), 59.2% of people who used other illegal drugs had not used cannabis first, and in Mexico (8.0%) 48.4%. Of the 15 countries with estimates, three (Japan, Nigeria, South Africa) exceeded 50%. (2) 'Other illegal drugs came before cannabis in ...': Table 4 counts people who had not already used cannabis when they began other illegal drugs, which includes people who never used cannabis. In Japan, other illegal drug use by 29 (2.4%) exceeded cannabis use (1.6%), so at least a third of the people who used other illegal drugs (unweighted, at least 5 of 16) had not used cannabis at all by 29 (editors' calculation). Wording: 'the order depended on how common each drug was' is stronger than the paper. For the order itself the authors report a descriptive correspondence across countries, with no formal test; country also stands for culture, reporting and sampling differences the authors could not control; 'varied with' fits better. Magnitude: the Netherlands-USA contrast (odds ratio 7.4 vs 107.1 at ages 18-29) does not illustrate 'weaker where cannabis was more common'. Cannabis use by 29 was more common in the USA (57.6% at 18-29, 40.9% overall) than in the Netherlands (38.9%, 18.4%), and in older Dutch cohorts the odds ratios were far higher (1,805.9 at 30-44, 2,015.4 at 45-59). The 'weaker where more common' finding rests only on the pooled interaction (0.3).
claims.note: Every number from this source was checked and is correct: 11.4% (USA, SE 1.2), 12.7% (New Zealand, SE 1.3), 83.2% (Japan, SE 10.9), 77.8% (Nigeria, SE 17.4), all in the Table 4 Total column and the text; 7.4 (1.8-30.4) and 107.1 (57.9-198.1), Table 3, ages 18-29; 0.3 (0.2-0.6) and 32.7 (8.3-129.0), Results 3.2 (prevalence scale not stated, as the claim says). '13 of 16' and '7 of 8' are the editors' pairing of Table 4 counts (people who had not used cannabis first) with Table 2 counts (people who used other illegal drugs by 29). The pairing is valid: in every country's Total column the Table 4 count does not exceed the Table 2 count. Unweighted 13/16 = 81.3% and 7/8 = 87.5%, against weighted 83.2% and 77.8%. Reporting inconsistency in the paper: for Nigeria aged 18-29, Table 4 has 3 people against 2 in Table 2. The odds ratios in Table 3 come from discrete-time survival models adjusted only for person-year and sex; the pooled interaction models added gender, age cohort and country. Also not in the claim: no significant interaction of alcohol or tobacco use with their prevalence for later cannabis initiation. The authors conclude the pattern 'at least partially' reflects unmeasured common causes, without ruling out causal effects, which fits the claim's 'evidence is insufficient'.

anchors.extracted: Use by age 29 (weighted): cannabis Japan 1.6% (n = 11), Nigeria 2.8% (71), Mexico 8.0%, South Africa 8.5% (called moderate; cross-country median 9.8%), Netherlands 18.4% (38.9% at 18-29), New Zealand 40.1%, USA 40.9% (57.6% at 18-29); other illegal drugs Japan 2.4% (n = 16), Nigeria 0.3% (n = 8). anchors.locator: Table 3, row 'Cannabis use and later Other illicit drug use' and table note; Results › 3.2 Cross-national and age cohort differences in associations between order of initiation of drug use and later other drug use, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Discrete-time survival models adjusted for person-year and sex, use by 29. Cannabis use and later other illegal drug use, odds ratio (95% CI): Netherlands 7.4 (1.8-30.4) at 18-29 but 1,805.9 (174.9-18,642.3) at 30-44 and 62.5 (9.6-406.5) overall; USA 107.1 (57.9-198.1) at 18-29 and 137.1 (94.8-198.3) overall; New Zealand 118.0 overall. With few exceptions earlier drugs predicted later ones, with strength differing between countries.

anchors.locator: Results › 3.2 Cross-national and age cohort differences in associations between order of initiation of drug use and later other drug use, 2nd paragraph (after Table 3); Method › 2.3 Analysis methods, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Pooled models with country, age cohort and gender as covariates: interaction of alcohol or tobacco use with alcohol or tobacco prevalence for later other illegal drug use, odds ratio 32.7 (8.3-129.0), stronger where those were more common; interaction of cannabis use with cannabis prevalence 0.3 (0.2-0.6), weaker where cannabis was more common; no significant interaction for later cannabis initiation. The prevalence scale is not stated.

anchors.locator: Table 5, 'Gateway violation' rows; Results › 3.3 Cross-national and cross-cohort differences in violations to the gateway sequence, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Starting in an unusual order (cannabis or other illegal drugs before both alcohol and tobacco; other illegal drugs before cannabis) largely did not predict onset of dependence; the only significant odds ratio was 1.6 (1.1-2.3) for other illegal drugs before cannabis and alcohol dependence.

The authors conclude that the gateway pattern at least partially reflects unmeasured common causes rather than effects of specific drugs, and that the strength of the associations may be driven by background prevalence rather than wholly explained by causal mechanisms. They describe the correspondence between prevalence and order violations across countries as remarkably good, and note that US cannabis users were much more likely than Dutch ones to go on to other illegal drugs.

anchors.locator: Method › 2.2.1 Order of onset and violations of the gateway progression, 1st paragraph and Violation 3
anchors.extracted: Order is taken from ages of first use recalled at one interview; Violation 3 is first use of other illegal drugs before cannabis. Same-year starts are not addressed.

Cross-sectional, retrospective recall; prevalence need not reflect supply, demand or attitudes; country used as the unit, with ethnic and religious groupings not controlled; differences in willingness to report may remain; no instrumental variables measured and no analysis able to estimate the causal effect of preventing early drug use.
